# The Parking Brake and Shifter Throb: Diagnosing a Nissan Altima Symptom

A clicking noise while parked that disappears once the vehicle is in motion, combined with a distinct throbbing sensation on the gear shifter, points to a specific mechanical isolation issue rather than a drivetrain failure. In your 2017 Nissan Altima, the fact that the noise occurs only when stationary and vanishes during driving or in Neutral eliminates the primary braking componentsâthe rotors, pads, and calipersâas the immediate suspect. If the issue were related to rotor warping or pad drag, you would feel resistance while rolling or hear grinding even when coasting. The symptom profile here is strictly tied to the parking brake assembly and its interface with the transmission mount.

When you engage the parking brake on an automatic transmission, the system relies on a mechanical linkage to hold the rear wheels. On many Nissans of this generation, that linkage connects to a small drum or cable mechanism inside the rear wheel assembly. If one side of the parking brake is binding more than the other, or if the internal adjuster has seized, you can create a torque imbalance. This imbalance manifests as a vibration or "throbbing" through the chassis structure when the brakes are fully applied and the engine is idling. The clicking sound is likely the mechanical ratchet engaging to lock the brake in place under that uneven load, similar to how a stuck window regulator might click if you try to force it against friction.

The throbbing felt on the shifter is the critical diagnostic clue. In your specific test case, placing a hand on the shifter confirmed that the vibration travels up through the transmission tunnel. This happens because the parking brake cables are anchored near the transmission bell housing. When the rear brakes grab unevenly, they create a torque reaction that twists the transmission mount slightly. The mount acts as a dampener, but if it is worn or if the braking force is high enough, that twist translates directly into the shifter lever. It is a structural vibration caused by the load, not an electrical signal or a software glitch.

You mentioned testing with the parking brake released and the noise persisting. If the clicking continues after releasing the manual parking lever but remains when the foot brake is pressed to the floor while stationary, you are now isolating the issue to the rear wheel cylinders or the parking brake cable tension itself. However, if the noise stops completely once the parking brake lever is disengaged and you leave the car in Park (P) without pressing the foot brake hard, then the issue is strictly a mechanical binding in the parking brake system that needs adjustment or replacement of the cables.

The trade-off here is between adjusting the cable tension versus replacing the rear brake assemblies. Adjusting the cable is the low-friction solution; it restores symmetry to the braking force. However, if the clicking persists after adjustment, the internal mechanism of one rear wheel might be corroded or damaged. Replacing the entire rear drum assembly is the high-assurance solution that eliminates any variable related to internal binding. Given the specific symptom of the shifter throbbing, ensuring both rear brakes apply with equal force is not just a noise fix; it prevents uneven wear on the transmission mounts and ensures the parking brake holds the vehicle securely on inclines without inducing chassis flex.

For a 2017 Altima, verifying the condition of the rear wheel cylinders is essential. If these hydraulic components are failing internally, they might apply pressure inconsistently when the mechanical parking brake tries to hold the car. This inconsistency creates the pulsating torque that you feel through the shifter. Addressing this early prevents potential dragging issues once the vehicle is back in motion, which could lead to premature wear on the front brake pads due to excessive heat generation from a rear-end imbalance.
